# Day 1 — Overview {#sec-day1}

Today you build a machine learning model that works, and then you break it.
Both halves matter. A model that works is a morning's work and most of you will
manage it before the first break. Knowing the conditions under which it stops
working is the part that distinguishes a health data scientist from someone who
can call `.fit()`.

The thread running through the day is a single clinical question:

> **Given a patient's age and illness severity on admission, how long will they
> stay in hospital?**

We will answer it, measure how well we answered it, and then find out what
happens when the hospital changes.

## Objectives

By the end of the day you should be able to, without looking anything up:

::: {.objective-list}
- Write the same data-wrangling, model-fitting and plotting step in both R and
  Python, and say which parts of your result are language-dependent.
- Name the five steps of a supervised learning pipeline and say what each one
  is protecting you against.
- Fit a regression model, evaluate it on held-out data, and compare it against
  a baseline that does no learning at all.
- Explain why a test-set score is not a promise about next year's patients.
- Distinguish a change in *who the patients are* from a change in *how the
  outcome arises*, using evidence rather than assertion, and say which of the
  two your model can survive.
:::

## Shape of the day

| | Exercise | Time | Mode |
|---|---------|------|------|
| 1.1 | [Two languages, one analysis](day1-01-two-languages.qmd) | 45 min | pairs |
| 1.2 | [Your first ML pipeline](day1-02-first-pipeline.qmd) | 60 min | individual |
| — | break | 15 min | |
| 1.3 | [When the patients change](day1-03-distribution-shift.qmd) | 60 min | pairs, then plenary |
| 1.4 | [Consolidation](day1-04-consolidation.qmd) | 20 min | plenary |

: {tbl-colwidths="[6,52,18,24]"}

Do them in order. Exercise 1.3 depends on the model built in Exercise 1.2 — it
rebuilds it in its first cell, but the argument only makes sense if you have
already fitted and evaluated it yourself.

## What you need before you start

- A browser. Nothing else: the code cells run in the page. If your connection
  is slow, open @sec-two-languages and press Run on the first cell before the
  session starts, so the runtime is cached.
- Module 2 linear regression: what a coefficient is, and what a residual is. You
  do **not** need anything about p-values today — we will not compute one.

::: {.callout-note}
## A note on what we are *not* doing today
We treat length of stay as a pure prediction problem: we want a number that is
close to the truth, and we do not ask whether age *causes* longer stays. That
restraint is doing real work. A model can predict well using a variable that
would be useless, or harmful, to intervene on. Causal questions arrive later in
the module; today, prediction only.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Running the day.** The three exercises are independent in content but
sequential in argument: 1.3 only bites if the student has personally watched the
model succeed in 1.2. A student who skips 1.2 should be told the test MAE and
the baseline before starting 1.3, not left to infer them.

**Where the time actually goes.** Exercise 1.1 overruns if students try to make
the two languages produce identical numbers; the callout about splits exists to
pre-empt that, but say it out loud as well. Exercise 1.3 Task 3 (refitting on
each extract) is where the day's learning happens — protect 20 minutes for it
even if that means dropping the stretch tasks in 1.2.

**Plenary.** Run the 1.3 debrief as a vote before revealing anything: ask for
hands on "which extract is the dangerous one". The split between those who
voted for B (patients changed most visibly) and C (rules changed) is the lesson,
and it is far more memorable than being told.
:::
:::
